newsitem.title: MALDIVES: S.Asian bloc sets free-trade goal, political talks.
newsitem.headline: S.Asian bloc sets free-trade goal, political talks.

text.p: The leaders of seven South Asian nations ended a three-day summit on Wednesday with a pledge to form a free-trade zone by 2001 and launch political talks to ease tensions which have hobbled regional cooperation.

The leaders of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) announced in a joint declaration that they had decided to bring forward the deadline for a free-trade area by four years to 2001.

They also agreed to initiate "informal political consultations" within SAARC, which in its 12 years has focused on economic and social cooperation, and sidestepped contentious bilateral disputes which have hampered regional integration.

"It will clear the air and build confidence," Maldivian President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom told a news conference at the end of the summit, which brought together the leaders of Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, Maldives, Nepal, Pakistan and Sri Lanka.
A half-century of tension between the bloc's biggest members, India and Pakistan, has been one of the main stumbling blocks to greater economic cooperation.
The prime ministers of India and Pakistan held positive bilateral talks on the sidelines of this week's summit on Monday.

The joint declaration said the heads of state or government had agreed that political dialogue would prove useful in "fostering good neighbourly relations, relieving tensions and building confidence".
"This is indeed an historic decision, one which takes SAARC into an area of new opportunities and great promise," Gayoom told delegates in the Maldivian capital, Male.

The SAARC leaders agreed to speed up the establishment of the South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) to 2001 from 2005, which Gayoom said would help ensure the region's 1.2 billion people benefit from its economic resources and trade potential.

"However, to make SAFTA effective, we must focus not only on the removal of trade barriers but also on the trade facilitation measures that would increase the economic linkages between our seven countries," the Maldivian leader said.

The SAARC member states decided that their civil aviation authorities would meet soon to establish direct air services between the nations' capitals "which would promote people-to-people contact and encourage tourism".
Recognising that SAARC has fallen short of its goals, the leaders ordered the formation of a Group of Eminent Persons to revitalise the 12-year-old bloc and set future goals.
The declaration said member states should move towards a regional treaty on the environment and share scientific talent to protect and manage it.
The statement called for stringent measures to protect children from exploitation and ordered the creation of a study group to examine the roots of the problem.
The SAARC leaders agreed that existing legislation in member states should be strengthened to combat the trafficking of women and children.
Gayoom said SAARC leaders, aware of the depth of poverty in the region, had resolved to bring tangible benefits to the people.
"There are a lot of reasons that countries of the SAARC have not been able to achieve much in the past," he said.

"But I think now with the emphasis on better education and better opportunities for our businesses and the resolve that we should achieve something for the people of the region, I think this summit could be a different one."
